Where the time went

Wind, sounded by thermal

  • measured from circle drift
  • model profile for the day

One point per climb, numbered as in the table below and therefore in the order flown — the first and last carry their clock time, and hovering any point gives the rest. Height is where the climb was worked; the tail points downwind. Reading it bottom to top: about 3 km/h throughout, with no useful shear between the low climbs and the high ones.

How strong was the lift you sat in?

Every second spent circling, sorted into half-metre climb-rate buckets. The tallest bar is the climb rate you spent the most time in — not the best one you found. Bars left of zero are time spent turning in sink. The right-hand tail is the cores. This day reads as mostly +0.8 m/s, best sustained about +4 m/s, 14% of the circling in sink.

Climbs

Turns is total heading change ÷ 360 — how many circles the climb took, nothing more. m/turn is what that buys you: height gained per circle, so a thermal worked tightly in the core shows more metres per turn than the same average climb ground out in wide circles. Eff is mean climb over the best 20 s of the same climb — the closest single number to “did you stay in the core”. Reversals and radius say how tidily it was flown.

The air that day

ERA5 reanalysis, surface only over the middle of the course line, valid 2018-09-28 12:00 UTC. Fetched once and embedded — the report makes no requests when you open it.

surface15 °Cdew 1 °C · spread 14 K
cloudbase3 954 mfrom the surface spread
boundary layer3 697 mmodel mixing depth
you reached3 774 mhighest point, GPS datum

No vertical profile is available for this date: the reanalysis archive serves surface fields for any past day but returns nothing on pressure levels, so the sounding and the wind comparison are missing here. Flights from the last two months get the full profile.

Model, not measurement. This is a model's analysis for a point near the course line, not a radiosonde ascent. Treat the ceilings as ±100 m and the winds as indicative.

How to read this, and what to distrust

Altitude is GPS. This recorder has no pressure sensor, so both altitude and climb come from GPS and are noisier than they look.

Phases come from comparing progress — straight-line distance over distance flown in a 20 s window — against climb rate. Above 0.9 is gliding; below it with lift is a climb. The heuristic is Tom Payne's, from igc2kmz.

Wind is inferred, not measured. While circling, the glider's own airspeed averages out and the track drifts with the air. Climbs flown fewer than two full turns, or in both directions, are excluded — they measure the pilot, not the wind.

Cross-checked against igc2kmz on this same file: it finds the same 13 climbs and 19 glides, with start times within 4 s. Both read the same GPS altitude here, so the heights agree.

The 19 glides and 13 climbs account for 82% of airtime. The rest is transitions too short or too ambiguous to call, which is honest rather than tidy.

Open-Meteo operational model over the middle of the course line, valid 2026-06-16 09:00 UTC. Fetched once and embedded — the report makes no requests when you open it.

No vertical profile is available for this date: the reanalysis archive serves surface fields for any past day but returns nothing on pressure levels, so the sounding and the wind comparison are missing here. Flights from the last two months get the full profile.

Model, not measurement. This is a model's analysis for a point near the course line, not a radiosonde ascent. Treat the ceilings as ±100 m and the winds as indicative.

How to read this, and what to distrust

Altitude is barometric. This recorder has a pressure sensor, so climb rates come from the smooth baro trace. It reads ISA pressure altitude, sitting 237 m below the GPS altitude on the day — absolute heights are indicative, height changes are solid.

Phases come from comparing progress — straight-line distance over distance flown in a 20 s window — against climb rate. Above 0.9 is gliding; below it with lift is a climb. The heuristic is Tom Payne's, from igc2kmz.

Wind is inferred, not measured. While circling, the glider's own airspeed averages out and the track drifts with the air. Climbs flown fewer than two full turns, or in both directions, are excluded — they measure the pilot, not the wind.

Cross-checked against igc2kmz on this same file: it finds the same 52 climbs and 60 glides, with start times within 4 s. Its altitude figures run higher because it prefers GPS altitude where this reads baro.

The 60 glides and 52 climbs account for 86% of airtime. The rest is transitions too short or too ambiguous to call, which is honest rather than tidy.

Your own tracks

Read in this page

Nothing is uploaded: the file is parsed and analysed here. Each track you add gets its own tab, and the × on a tab removes that flight again.

.igc preferred · or drag them here · .kml and .kmz also read

A KMZ downloaded from a scoring site is usually reduced to 500 points — every few minutes on a long flight. Distances, height gained and turn counts are all measured along the track, so they come out low, and turns cannot be counted at all. The IGC your instrument recorded is the file to use.
